Choosing the Right Backpack for a Week-Long Trek

Picking a backpack for a multi-day trek is less about the brand on the label and more about how the pack sits against your own back once it is loaded with water, food, and shelter. Most people buy on capacity alone, then discover three days in that the hip belt is digging into their pelvis or the frame is transferring almost none of the load off their shoulders. Before anything else, get measured for torso length at an outfitter that actually stocks multiple frame sizes, because a pack that fits your friend perfectly can be genuinely painful on a different body.

Capacity matters too, but less than most first-time buyers assume. A five-day summer trip in a warm climate can be comfortable in a 45-liter pack if you are disciplined about what you bring, while a shoulder-season trip with a heavier sleep system and more layers can overflow a 60-liter pack. Rather than picking a liter number first, lay out everything you plan to carry, including food and water for the driest stretch of the route, and pack it into a rental or borrowed bag before you commit to a purchase. This single step catches more mistakes than reading a dozen comparison articles.

Once fit and capacity are settled, the remaining decisions are mostly about durability and weight trade-offs. Ultralight packs shave weight by removing structure, which is fine on well-maintained trails but can feel flimsy scrambling over talus. Heavier packs with rigid frames carry big loads more comfortably but punish you on long approach hikes before the trail even starts. There is no universal right answer here, only a right answer for the specific trip you are planning and the terrain you expect to cross. Buy for the trips you actually take, not the trip you imagine taking once a year.

Finally, break the pack in before a real trip. Load it to its expected weight, walk a few miles on pavement, then a few more on uneven ground, and adjust every strap more than once. Small adjustments compound over eight hours of walking, and what feels fine for twenty minutes in a store can become unbearable by the second day on trail. A short shakedown hike close to home is worth far more than another hour spent comparing spec sheets online.
